problem: Point-goal urban navigation methods (e.g. CityWalker) break down when consumer navigation-tool routes (Google Maps / Amap) are coarse and geometrically misaligned with the real world, and existing navigation VLAs are not built for long-range, rule-abiding, safety-critical urban micromobility.
motivation: Urban micromobility platforms such as delivery robots, wheelchairs and guide robots need scalable navigation without HD maps, in dynamic pedestrian spaces. Navigation-app routes give cheap global guidance but are noisy, so the policy must learn to align routes with visual observations and rely on vision for local safety.
key_idea: A route-conditioned VLA (built on NavFoM) takes noisy roadbook waypoints plus multi-camera RGB and predicts trajectory waypoints, trained with SFT on lifted noisy routes from simulation and web video, followed by IQL offline RL on sim and real teleoperation data.
insight: Training on heuristically lifted, noised routes (HTL) prevents overfitting to the route input: without HTL, simulation SR is slightly higher (93% vs 89%) but real-world route completion on a C-shaped sidewalk with a ~10 m route offset falls from 100% to 42%. IQL-based RFT adds gains that are larger on unseen scenes (SR 82%→88%, cost 0.98→0.82). Mid-layer LLM hidden states (layer 17) are reported to give more stable Q-values than top-layer states, though no ablation table is shown.
method: Route encoding: resample the upcoming 40 m of the route at 2 m spacing (20 waypoints) in the robot frame, plus block-level 'turn right in 30 m' cues, and fill an instruction template; at deployment these come from the Amap API.

VLA architecture: NavFoM base, DINOv2+SigLIP features with grid pooling and a 2-layer MLP projector, Qwen2 LLM with a sliding window of k frames over multiple cameras; an MLP action head decodes the action token into N SE(2) waypoints, and a language head handles VideoQA.

Heuristic Trajectory Lifting (HTL): Savitzky-Golay denoising, filtering of self-intersecting paths, window-based corner detection, segmenting, Gaussian positional noise per segment, then merging and resampling into an abstract noisy route from raw simulator or web trajectories.
SFT: MSE loss on navigation data (MetaUrban PPO-expert trajectories and Sekai web videos) jointly with cross-entropy VideoQA (LongVU, Sekai) to keep real-world scene understanding.

IQL reinforcement fine-tuning: Q and V networks take the layer-17 last-token LLM hidden state as state and the vectorized trajectory (3N) as action; the policy is updated with an advantage-weighted regression loss exp(βA)·||a-π(s)||².
Reward: 0.5·completion increment − 1·collision − 1·deviation from the route corridor, computable in both sim and real (via UI annotation or LiDAR odometry).
Sim-real RFT dataset: 2,400 MetaUrban episodes (~40 h, PPO expert) plus ~8 h of real human teleoperation, including scenes where the navigation info is inconsistent with reality.

setting.backbone: NavFoM (Qwen2 LLM + DINOv2/SigLIP), fine-tuned with SFT then IQL
setting.training_data: MetaUrban PPO-expert trajectories, Sekai web navigation videos (HTL-lifted routes), VideoQA data from LongVU and Sekai; RFT on 2,400 sim episodes (~40 h) plus ~8 h real teleoperation; 96 GPU hours on 8 H100
setting.observation: multi-view RGB (4 cameras on the real robot: front, left, right, rear) plus route waypoints and turn instructions; GNSS for route localization
setting.action_space: predicted SE(2) trajectory waypoints (max step distance 1.5 m in MetaUrban evaluation)
setting.privileged: none at test time in the benchmark beyond the simulator's route; the real robot uses Amap routes and GNSS

numbers_note: Table 1 reports 91%/0.80 (test) in the Table 1 row as 91%/0.81 and in Table 3 as 91%/0.80 for the SocialNav SFT+RFT model (minor cost inconsistency within the paper); Table 3 unseen SR 88%/cost 0.82. The intro/text also mistakenly states PointNav unseen numbers as 'test' numbers. Real-world results are qualitative except the HTL ablation (RC 100% with HTL vs 42% without, 10 trials).
results: On MetaUrban, RGB-only UrbanVLA reaches PointNav SR 94% (test) / 97% (unseen) and SocialNav SR 91% / 88%, far above LiDAR-based baselines (best baseline SocialNav SR 36% / 32%; best PointNav SR 66% / 60%). It has higher cumulative cost than some safe-RL baselines such as PPO-Lag. Real-world deployment on a Unitree Go2 with Amap routes works over 500 m routes, including overpasses, crossings and night scenes.
limitations: Cumulative cost is higher than several baselines (e.g. PPO-Lag), and baselines use LiDAR while the VLA uses RGB, so the comparison is not like-for-like; the action space and step size were also adapted.
Real-world evaluation is mostly qualitative, with only a small quantitative test (a single C-shaped sidewalk, 10 trials); inference runs on a remote server at 2 Hz.
Reward and RFT rely on human teleoperation and annotation data, and only ~8 h of real data are used.
